How to Price a Freelance Retainer: The $1,600-a-Month Formula, Worked Out Step by Step

Direct AnswerPrice a freelance retainer from your floor rate, not a discount: 20 hours at $80 an hour is $1,600 a month. Rollover, overage, capacity and renewal math.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 6, 2026•12 min read•Calculation Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: $1,600 a MonthWhat a Retainer Actually IsStart From Your Floor Rate, Not a DiscountThe Retainer Formula: Hours × Rate, Plus a PremiumWhat Retainers Actually Cost by Service TypeUnused Hours: The Rollover DebtOverage: The Clause That Protects the FeeHow Many Retainers Fit in Your MonthHours or Deliverables: Which Way to Price ItWhat $1,600 a Month Is Worth in a YearRaising the Retainer at RenewalRetainer vs Hourly vs ProjectHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

A freelance retainer for 20 hours a month at an $80-an-hour floor rate is $1,600 a month — $1,840 with a 15% premium for guaranteed availability. The formula is one line: monthly retainer = reserved hours × floor rate, plus a premium for the access the client is buying. A discount is not in the formula — a 10% discount drops the effective rate to $72 an hour, below the floor. The rest of this guide prices every term that decides whether that $1,600 still works in month twelve: rollover, overage, capacity, the annual value, and the renewal raise.

The Short Answer: $1,600 a Month

The question behind this guide is the one freelancers actually type: "how much should I charge for a monthly retainer?" The answer is not a market average — it is your own floor rate, multiplied by the hours you are reserving. A retainer is a price for reserved capacity: the client pays a fixed monthly fee, and in return a block of your time is theirs, whether they use all of it or not. Here is the whole answer on one freelancer, worked out step by step:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Floor rate from the income goal$95,555.56 required revenue ÷ 1,200 billable hours$79.63 an hour
Step 2 — Round the floor up to a quotable rate$79.63 → $80.00$80.00 an hour
Step 3 — Reserved hours for this client20 hours a month20 hours
Step 4 — Base monthly retainer20 × $80.00$1,600.00
Step 5 — Priority premium for guaranteed availability$1,600.00 × 15%$240.00
Step 6 — Quoted retainer, paid in advance$1,600.00 + $240.00$1,840.00 a month

Two things to notice. First, the $1,600 base is not a guess: the $79.63 floor rate comes from the same calculation our freelance rate calculator runs — a $60,000 income goal, a 25% tax reserve, $6,000 of expenses, a 10% profit margin, and 25 billable hours a week over 48 weeks, which is $95,555.56 of required revenue over 1,200 billable hours. Rounding the floor up to $80 is the only rounding in the whole chain, and it works in your favour. Second, the $240 premium is the price of the promise, not the hours: the client is buying the guarantee that you answer first and deliver first, and that guarantee has a price even in a month when they use only 14 of their 20 hours. The honesty note: this is a planning figure for a US freelancer, before taxes — the annual-value section below sets aside the tax reserve, and the limitations section lists what the fee does not cover.

What a Retainer Actually Is

A freelance retainer is a recurring monthly agreement: the client pays a fixed fee at the start of each month, and in exchange a defined slice of your time — or a defined set of deliverables — is reserved for them. It is not a salary, not a project fee, and not an hourly contract with a nicer name. The client is buying three things at once, and the price has to cover all three:

  • A block of output. The hours or deliverables the fee covers — 20 hours, or 4 blog posts, or 2 design sprints a month. This is the part the client can count.
  • Guaranteed availability. The promise that your time is there when they need it, ahead of project clients who book week by week. This is the part that justifies a premium rather than a discount.
  • Accumulated knowledge. You already know their brand, their systems, and their customers, so the first hour of every month is productive instead of onboarding. This is the part a new freelancer cannot sell yet.

The most common pricing mistake is charging for only the first item. A retainer quoted as "20 hours × $80" is honest about the output and silent about the other two — and that is how freelancers end up locked into a rate that falls below their floor the moment a client uses the hours badly. The premium in the short answer exists to price the second item. The third item is what makes the fee rise at renewal: after six months on a retainer, you are worth more to that client than a stranger with the same hourly rate, because you no longer need the first week to learn the business. The rest of this guide prices each term that protects that value.

Start From Your Floor Rate, Not a Discount

A retainer priced below your floor rate is a subscription to your own underpayment — you have simply agreed, in writing, to earn less than your plan requires, every month, for as long as the agreement lasts. So the first step is not the retainer at all: it is the floor rate, worked backwards from your income goal. Our freelance rate calculator runs exactly this calculation, and its worked example is the anchor for everything in this guide:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross up the income goal for tax$60,000.00 ÷ (1 − 0.25)$80,000.00
Step 2 — Add business expenses$80,000.00 + $6,000.00$86,000.00
Step 3 — Gross up for the profit margin$86,000.00 ÷ (1 − 0.10)$95,555.56 a year
Step 4 — Billable hours in the year25 hours × 48 weeks1,200 hours
Step 5 — Floor rate$95,555.56 ÷ 1,200$79.63 an hour
Step 6 — Full-capacity monthly retainer$95,555.56 ÷ 12$7,962.96 a month

The $7,962.96 figure is the calculator's own monthly-retainer output: it is what a single client would have to pay to reserve all of your billable capacity — all 100 hours a month. Nobody quotes that, because a retainer is a slice of capacity, not the whole month. But the number is useful as a ceiling: it tells you what your time is worth if it were fully sold, and it makes the $1,600 fee look like what it is — 20% of your monthly capacity, priced at the floor. Two checks before you move on. First, the 25% tax reserve is your own planning assumption, not a tax calculation — the annual-value section below works out what it means on a real retainer. Second, the floor rate is personal: change the income goal to $75,000 with the same expenses and margin and the required revenue becomes $117,777.78, the floor rate $98.15 an hour, and the same 20-hour retainer $1,963.00 a month. Never copy another freelancer's fee; copy the method.

The Retainer Formula: Hours × Rate, Plus a Premium

With the floor rate settled, the retainer formula is one line: monthly retainer = reserved hours × floor rate, plus a premium for guaranteed availability. The premium is what most quick calculators leave out, and it is the difference between a retainer that holds its value and one that quietly becomes a discount. The table below prices the same three retainer sizes three ways — at the floor, with a 15% priority premium, and with a 10% volume discount — so the trade-off is visible in dollars:

Reserved hours / monthAt the $80 floorWith 15% priority premiumWith 10% volume discountEffective rate at the discount
10 hours$800.00$920.00$720.00$72.00 an hour
20 hours$1,600.00$1,840.00$1,440.00$72.00 an hour
40 hours$3,200.00$3,680.00$2,880.00$72.00 an hour

The discount column is the warning. A 10% discount always lands at $72 an hour on an $80 floor, whatever the size — $80 a month given away on a 10-hour retainer, $160 on a 20-hour one, $320 on a 40-hour one. Over a year, the 20-hour discount costs $1,920.00 for the same 240 hours. The premium column is the mirror image: $120, $240, or $480 a month for the same hours, paid because the client can count on you. Which one you quote depends on what the client is actually buying. A client who wants a fixed number of deliverables on a fixed schedule is buying output, and the floor rate is the honest price. A client who wants a guaranteed response time, priority turnaround, and the right to call you first is buying access, and the premium is the honest price. What no client is buying is a discount for nothing — if they want 10% off, the trade has to be real: a 6- or 12-month commitment, payment in advance on the 1st of the month, or a scope narrow enough that your admin time falls. Our salary comparison calculator shows the employee side of the same question — what a $1,600-a-month retainer would have to replace if you gave up a salary for it — and our part-time conversion guide prices the same hours-to-annual math from the employee side.

What Retainers Actually Cost by Service Type

The $1,600 anchor is one freelancer's price, not a market rate. What clients actually pay varies by the kind of work, because the work varies in how much of it is hours and how much is judgement. The ranges below are the typical monthly figures reported across 2026 freelancer pricing guides — use them to sanity-check your fee, not to set it. Your floor rate still governs: a $1,500 retainer at a $100 floor rate is only 15 hours of work, and a $6,000 retainer at a $60 floor rate is 100 hours — the whole month.

Retainer typeTypical monthly rangeWhat drives the priceLimitations
Content marketing$1,500 – $6,000Volume, strategy depth, channelsPrice per deliverable set, not per word
Design (web / UI)$75 – $150 an hourSeniority, revision rounds, turnaroundHourly ranges hide the scope; quote the set
SEO / growth$1,500 – $5,000Reporting depth, technical scopeResults take months; the fee buys work, not rank
Strategic advisory / access$2,500 – $6,000Access hours, decision stakesMostly judgement; hours are the wrong unit
Virtual assistant$600 – $2,500Hours blocked, task complexitySmallest retainers; admin overhead is the risk

Read the table as a check, not a target. If your 20-hour design retainer comes out at $1,600 and the typical design range is $75 to $150 an hour, your $80 floor sits at the low end of the range — which is fine if the client is long-term and the scope is clean, and a signal to raise the fee at renewal if the scope keeps growing. If your content retainer comes out at $800 for 10 hours and the typical range starts at $1,500, the gap is not a reason to double the fee: it is a reason to check whether your floor rate covers your real costs, or whether the typical retainer buys twice the volume you are offering. The ranges also show why the minimum matters: a $600 virtual-assistant retainer at an $80 floor rate is 7.5 hours, below the 8-hour minimum in the FAQ — the admin eats the margin before the work starts.

Unused Hours: The Rollover Debt

Rollover is where good retainers go to die. The question is simple — the client paid for 20 hours and used 14; do the other 6 hours carry into next month? — and the answer decides whether your effective rate survives the year. The default in your agreement should be use-it-or-lose-it: the client pays for reserved capacity, and the hours expire at the end of the billing period, because you held the time whether they used it or not. If a client insists on rollover, cap it: one month only, and at most 25% of the monthly hours. Here is what the cap costs on the $1,600 anchor:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Hours banked under a 25% cap25% × 20 hours5 hours
Step 2 — Hours worked next month20 reserved + 5 banked25 hours
Step 3 — Fee for that monthUnchanged$1,600.00
Step 4 — Effective rate that month$1,600.00 ÷ 25$64.00 an hour
Step 5 — Value given away free5 × $80.00$400.00
Step 6 — If rollover were unlimited (10 banked)$1,600.00 ÷ 30$53.33 an hour

The $64.00 effective rate is $16 an hour below the $80 floor — the client got a 20% discount they never negotiated, and you worked a full extra day for nothing. Unlimited rollover is worse: the banked hours pile up silently, the client eventually calls them in all at once — usually in your busiest month — and you owe 30 hours of work for a 20-hour fee. The fix is not to refuse rollover outright. It is to price it: a one-month cap, a 25% ceiling, and a monthly report that shows exactly what the hours produced, so unused hours are visible before they become a debt. And if the client keeps using fewer hours than the retainer covers, that is not a rollover problem — it is a sizing problem. Shrink the retainer to 15 hours ($1,200) at the next renewal and free 5 hours a month for a client who will use them.

Overage: The Clause That Protects the Fee

If rollover is the slow leak, overage is the flood. Every retainer needs a written overage rate — what extra hours cost — because without one, the client will consistently push beyond the agreed scope and you will absorb it. The rule: overage costs your standard rate plus 10 to 20%, with no retainer discount applied. On the $80 floor rate, a 15% premium makes overage $92 an hour. The premium is deliberate: if extra hours cost the same as included hours, the rational client under-buys the retainer and tops up as needed, and you lose the predictability the retainer was supposed to buy. Two months on the same 20-hour, $1,600 retainer show how the clause works:

MonthHours usedRetainer feeOverageMonth totalEffective rate
Month 1 — light month14 of 20$1,600.00$0.00$1,600.00$114.29 an hour
Month 2 — heavy month26 (6 over)$1,600.006 × $92.00 = $552.00$2,152.00$82.77 an hour
Month 2 without the clause26 (6 free)$1,600.00$0.00$1,600.00$61.54 an hour

Month 1 is the retainer working as designed: the client paid for availability and used less than they reserved, so your effective rate is $114.29 an hour — the premium for holding the time. Month 2 is the overage clause earning its keep: the client used 6 hours more than the retainer covers, paid $552 for them, and your effective rate is $82.77 an hour — still above the $80 floor. The third row is the same month without the clause: 6 free hours, $1,600 for 26 hours of work, a $61.54 effective rate — $18.46 below the floor, and $552 of value handed over. Two habits make the clause stick. First, authorisation: extra hours need the client's sign-off before you work them, not a surprise line on the invoice. Second, the pattern rule: if the client goes over two months in a row, propose a larger retainer at the next review instead of billing overage every month — a 25-hour retainer at $2,000 a month is a better deal for both sides than a 20-hour retainer plus $552 of overage.

How Many Retainers Fit in Your Month

A retainer is not free money on top of your project work. It is a reservation against the same fixed pool of billable hours, and the pool is smaller than most freelancers think. The anchor freelancer has 25 billable hours a week over 48 weeks: 1,200 hours a year, 100 hours a month. The other 15 hours a week — admin, proposals, marketing, invoicing, learning — are real work that no client pays for directly, and they do not shrink because a client signed a retainer. Here is what three retainers do to that month:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Billable capacity per month1,200 ÷ 12100 hours
Step 2 — Retainer A (design, 20 hrs)20 × $80.00$1,600.00
Step 3 — Retainer B (content, 20 hrs)20 × $80.00$1,600.00
Step 4 — Retainer C (support, 15 hrs)15 × $80.00$1,200.00
Step 5 — Reserved hours and baseline fees55 hours; $1,600 + $1,600 + $1,20055 hours; $4,400.00 a month
Step 6 — Baseline annual revenue$4,400.00 × 12$52,800.00 a year
Step 7 — Hours left for project work100 − 5545 hours a month
Step 8 — Project headroom at the floor rate45 × $80.00$3,600.00 a month
Step 9 — Full-month potential$4,400.00 + $3,600.00$8,000.00 a month; $96,000.00 a year

The $96,000.00 full-month potential sits $444.44 above the $95,555.56 required revenue — which is the check that the plan works: three retainers covering 55% of capacity, plus project work filling the rest, clear the income goal with a small margin. The danger is at the edges. Four 20-hour retainers reserve 80 hours — 80% of capacity — and leave 20 hours a month for everything else, including overage; one heavy month across two clients and the week is gone. Five 20-hour retainers reserve all 100 hours: there is no room for a holiday, a sick week, or a single overage hour, and any rollover debt lands on hours that do not exist. The practical rule: keep reserved hours at or below 60% of capacity, and treat the remaining 40% as the buffer that makes the retainers survivable. That buffer is also where growth lives — it is the hours you sell as projects at the full rate, without a discount and without a commitment.

Hours or Deliverables: Which Way to Price It

Not every retainer should be priced in hours. A client who wants a predictable output — blog posts, social campaigns, design sprints — is better served by a deliverable-based retainer: a fixed set of outputs each month for a fixed fee, with extra outputs priced separately. The fee is the same; the unit changes. Four blog posts a month, each taking about 5 hours at the $80 floor rate, is $400 a post and $1,600 a month — the same anchor fee, quoted as output instead of time:

Retainer modelWhat the client buysMonthly feeExtra unitLimitations
Hours-based20 reserved hours$1,600.001 hour at $92.00 overageClient must track hours; scope can drift
Deliverable-based4 blog posts a month$1,600.001 extra post at $460.00Each post needs a size limit, or it grows
Access-basedPriority response + weekly call$1,840.00Additional day at $637.04Hardest to scope; needs a response-time line

The extra-post price of $460.00 is the same 15% premium as the hourly overage — $400 × 1.15 — applied to the deliverable instead of the hour. The access-based row is the third model: a client buying guaranteed availability and a weekly strategy call rather than hours or posts, priced at the $1,840 premium fee, with an extra day priced at the $637.04 day rate from the floor-rate calculation ($79.63 × 8). Which model to choose comes down to what the client can check. If they can count posts, quote posts. If they can count hours, quote hours. If what they really want is you, on call, quote access — and write the response time into the agreement, because "priority" without a number is a dispute waiting for a busy week. Whichever model you choose, the floor rate still governs the fee: a deliverable that takes 8 hours is a $640 deliverable, not a $400 one, and pricing it at $400 is a discount by another name.

What $1,600 a Month Is Worth in a Year

A monthly fee looks small until it is annualised. The $1,600 retainer is $19,200.00 a year of gross revenue if it stays active and paid for all twelve months — and "if" is doing real work in that sentence, because a retainer that ends in month seven is $11,200.00, not $19,200.00. Against the anchor freelancer's $95,555.56 required revenue, one $1,600 retainer is 20.09% of the year's target: five of them, at full capacity, would clear the goal — which is exactly why the capacity section says not to sell five. The annual figure also has to survive tax. A freelancer's retainer income is self-employment income, and the set-aside for it is the same tax reserve the floor rate was built on:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Annual gross from the retainer$1,600.00 × 12$19,200.00
Step 2 — Tax reserve at 25%$19,200.00 × 25%$4,800.00 set aside
Step 3 — Tax reserve at 30%$19,200.00 × 30%$5,760.00 set aside
Step 4 — Self-employment tax inside the reserve92.35% × $19,200.00 × 15.3%$2,712.87
Step 5 — Share of the year's required revenue$19,200.00 ÷ $95,555.5620.09%

The self-employment tax line is the one new freelancers miss: 15.3% applied to 92.35% of net earnings — about 14.13% effective — before income tax, which is why a 25–30% reserve is the common planning range and why the calculator's worked example uses 25%. On $19,200.00 of retainer income the self-employment tax alone is $2,712.87, and the rest of the reserve covers federal and state income tax. Two practical habits follow. First, move the reserve when the invoice is paid, not at tax time — a separate account, 25% of every retainer payment, on the day it lands. Second, remember the fee is gross: the $1,600 that looks like $1,600 a month is $1,200.00 a month after a 25% reserve, and the budget should be built on the second number. Our FICA guide explains the 7.65% employee-side layer the self-employment tax replaces, and our 401(k) guide shows the other side of the same coin — what a freelancer can shelter instead of reserving.

Raising the Retainer at Renewal

A retainer that never rises is a pay cut in slow motion: your costs rise, your knowledge of the client deepens, and the fee stays where it was on the day you were least sure of your value. The raise happens at renewal, not mid-term, and it is quoted as a new fee, not a new rate — clients accept "$1,760 a month" more easily than "$88 an hour", because the fee is what they budget and the rate is what you earn. The anchor raise is 10%:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — New floor rate after a 10% raise$80.00 × 1.10$88.00 an hour
Step 2 — New monthly fee, same 20 hours20 × $88.00$1,760.00 a month
Step 3 — Extra income per month$1,760.00 − $1,600.00$160.00
Step 4 — Extra income per year$160.00 × 12$1,920.00

The trigger for the conversation is the quarterly audit, and it is a number, not a feeling. Track your effective rate every month — fee divided by hours actually worked, including overage — and if it drifts more than 15% below your floor for two consecutive months, the retainer is mispriced. On an $80 floor the trigger line is $68.00 an hour: two months under it, and the next renewal carries a raise or a smaller scope. Give 30 days of written notice, tie the raise to something the client can see — the scope grew, the response time shortened, the volume doubled — and offer the choice: the new fee for the same hours, or the old fee for fewer hours. A client who chooses fewer hours has just told you the retainer was oversized, which is useful information either way. And if the client refuses both, let the retainer end: a $1,600 retainer that costs $1,920 a year in lost increases is a client you are subsidising.

Retainer vs Hourly vs Project

The retainer is one of three ways to sell the same work, and the right one depends on who carries the risk when the work takes longer than planned. Hourly pricing sends the overrun cost to the client, provided they authorised the hours. A fixed project fee keeps it with you. A retainer can go either way, depending on one clause: the overage clause. The same 40-hour deliverable, estimated at the $80 floor rate, priced three ways — and then run 50% over, to 60 hours — shows the difference:

Pricing modelQuoted fee (40 hrs)Paid at 60 hrs, with sign-offPaid at 60 hrs, without sign-offLimitations
Hourly$3,200.00$4,800.00 ($80.00 an hour)$3,200.00 (unpaid hours)Client carries overruns only if they authorise them
Fixed project fee$3,840.00 (20% allowance)$3,840.00 ($64.00 an hour)$3,840.00 ($64.00 an hour)You carry every overrun; scope must be exact
Retainer (32 hrs + overage)$2,560.00 a month$4,800.00 ($80.00 an hour)$2,560.00 ($42.67 an hour)Without an overage clause, the retainer is the worst of the three

The retainer row is the warning that runs through this whole guide: with an overage clause and the client's sign-off, the retainer pays the full $80 an hour at 60 hours, same as hourly. Without the clause, the same 60 hours pay $42.67 an hour — below the floor, below the fixed fee, and below the minimum wage logic of the whole business. That is why the overage clause is the single most important line in a retainer agreement: it is the line that decides who pays when the work grows. Choose hourly when the scope is unknowable, fixed fee when the scope is exact and the estimate is padded, and a retainer when the client needs the same kind of work every month and you can say in one line what the fee buys — a set output, a block of hours, or guaranteed response times. Our pay-stub guide shows where retainer income lands if you ever take it as an employee instead, and our bonus-tax guide prices the lump-sum alternative — a one-off payment instead of a monthly commitment.

How to Use the Calculator

Price your own retainer in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Find your floor rate first in the freelance rate calculator: enter your income goal, your tax reserve, your business expenses, your profit margin, and the billable hours you can realistically sell each week. The calculator returns the rate your plan requires — and the monthly retainer for reserving all of it.
  2. Step 2 — Multiply the floor rate by the hours you are reserving: 20 hours at an $80 floor is a $1,600 base. Round the floor rate up to a quotable number before you multiply, never down.
  3. Step 3 — Add the premium or the discount, never both: 15% for guaranteed availability and priority turnaround, or a discount only for a real trade — a 6- or 12-month commitment, or payment in advance. Check the effective rate against your floor before you quote.
  4. Step 4 — Test the terms before you sign: run one light month (14 of 20 hours) and one heavy month (26 hours with overage) through the numbers. If the effective rate stays above your floor in both, the retainer is priced right.

Limitations

  1. Planning figures, not market rates: the $80 floor rate and the $1,600 fee come from one freelancer's income goal, expenses, and billable hours. Your floor rate is personal — change any input and the fee changes with it — and the service-type ranges are typical figures reported by other guides, not verified market data.
  2. Gross, before tax: every fee in this guide is gross revenue. Self-employment tax (15.3% on 92.35% of net earnings), federal income tax, and state income tax all come out of it, which is why the 25–30% reserve is part of the method and not an afterthought.
  3. Billable hours are the constraint: the capacity math assumes 25 billable hours a week over 48 weeks. If your real billable hours are 15 a week, your floor rate is higher, your capacity is 60 hours a month, and three 20-hour retainers already fill it.
  4. Terms are general information, not legal advice: rollover caps, overage rates, notice periods, and payment-in-advance clauses are points to agree with your client in writing. Have your own agreement reviewed where the amount at stake justifies it, and check your state's rules on independent-contractor agreements.
  5. Retainers end: the $19,200 annual value assumes the retainer stays active and paid for all twelve months. A retainer that ends in month seven is worth $11,200, and the capacity it frees is only valuable if you can sell it again.
  6. Not tax or financial advice: these are 2026 planning estimates using the site's own freelance-rate method. Your actual tax depends on your circumstances, deductions, and jurisdiction, and the right rate for you depends on your whole budget.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about pricing a freelance retainer:

How much should I charge for a monthly retainer?

Start from your floor rate — the hourly rate your income goal actually requires — then multiply it by the hours you are reserving. At an $80-an-hour floor rate, 20 hours a month is a $1,600 monthly retainer, and a 15% priority premium for guaranteed availability takes it to $1,840. A discount is not part of the formula: a 10% discount on the same retainer drops the effective rate to $72 an hour, below the $80 floor, which means you are paying the client for the privilege of steady work. Check the fee against your floor rate before you quote it, and quote the fee as a flat monthly number, not as an hourly rate.

Do unused retainer hours roll over to the next month?

Only if your agreement says so, and the default should be that they do not. A retainer buys reserved capacity, not hours banked for later: the client pays for the guarantee that your time is there, whether they use it or not. If you allow rollover, cap it at one month and at 25% of the monthly hours. On a 20-hour, $1,600 retainer, 5 banked hours used the next month means you work 25 hours for $1,600 — a $64-an-hour effective rate, $16 below an $80 floor — and the 5 free hours are $400 of value given away. Unlimited rollover is worse: 10 banked hours drops the effective rate to $53.33 an hour.

How do I charge for hours beyond the retainer?

With an overage rate written into the agreement before the work starts: your standard rate plus 10 to 20%. At an $80 floor rate, a 15% premium makes overage $92 an hour. In a month where the client uses 26 hours on a 20-hour, $1,600 retainer, the 6 overage hours add $552, the month totals $2,152, and your effective rate is $82.77 an hour — still above the floor. Without an overage clause, those 6 hours are free, the effective rate falls to $61.54 an hour, and the client has no reason to size the retainer correctly next month.

Should I give a discount for a retainer?

Only in exchange for something real, and never below your floor rate. A 10% discount on a $1,600 retainer is $1,440 a month — $72 an hour on an $80 floor — so the discount costs you $160 a month, $1,920 a year, for the same 20 hours. What justifies it is a real trade: a 6- or 12-month commitment, payment in advance on the 1st, or a scope narrow enough to cut your admin time. If the client offers nothing in return, price the retainer at the floor rate and add a premium for guaranteed availability instead — $1,840 at a 15% premium — which is what the client is actually buying.

How many hours should a retainer include?

At least 8 hours a month. Below that, the admin of onboarding, monthly billing, tracking a work log, and managing the relationship eats a meaningful share of the fee — at $80 an hour, 8 hours is a $640-a-month minimum. The common range is 10 to 40 hours a month: 10 hours is $800, 20 hours is $1,600, and 40 hours is $3,200 at the same rate. The real ceiling is your capacity: at 25 billable hours a week over 48 weeks you have 100 billable hours a month, so five 20-hour retainers fill the month completely and leave no room for project work or overage.

How do I raise my retainer rate?

At renewal, with 30 days of written notice, and by quoting the new fee, not the new rate. A 10% raise on an $80 floor rate takes the rate to $88 an hour, so a 20-hour retainer moves from $1,600 to $1,760 a month — $160 more a month, $1,920 more a year — for the same hours. The trigger for the conversation is your quarterly audit: track your effective rate every month, and if it drifts more than 15% below your floor — under $68 an hour on an $80 floor — for two consecutive months, raise the fee or shrink the scope at the next renewal. Never raise a retainer mid-term unless the agreement allows it.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • 20 hours at an $80 floor rate is a $1,600-a-month retainer — $1,840 with a 15% priority premium — and the floor rate comes from your income goal, not from a market average: $95,555.56 of required revenue over 1,200 billable hours is $79.63 an hour.
  • A 10% discount always lands below the floor — $1,440 a month, $72 an hour on an $80 floor — and costs $1,920 a year on a 20-hour retainer for the same 240 hours. Discount only for a real trade: a long commitment or payment in advance.
  • Cap rollover at one month and 25% of the hours — 5 banked hours used the next month drop the effective rate to $64 an hour and give away $400 of value; unlimited rollover drops it to $53.33.
  • Overage at your rate plus 10 to 20% is the clause that protects the fee — $92 an hour on an $80 floor keeps a 26-hour month at $82.77 an hour; without the clause the same month pays $61.54.
  • Keep reserved hours at or below 60% of capacity — three retainers totalling 55 of 100 billable hours a month leave a $4,400 baseline and $3,600 of project headroom, $96,000 a year of potential against $95,555.56 required.
  • A $1,600 retainer is $19,200 a year, 20.09% of the year's target — set aside 25% ($4,800), including $2,712.87 of self-employment tax, and budget on the $1,200 a month that remains.
  • Raise the fee at renewal, never mid-term — 10% takes the retainer from $1,600 to $1,760 a month, $1,920 more a year, and two consecutive months under a $68 effective rate is the trigger to ask.
  • Never sell a retainer without an overage clause — a 60-hour month without one pays $42.67 an hour, the worst of all three pricing models, and the client has no reason to size the retainer correctly next month.

Sources & Method

Floor-rate method: the site's own freelance rate calculator — required revenue = [income goal ÷ (1 − tax reserve) + expenses] ÷ (1 − profit margin), divided by billable hours. The anchor uses the calculator's own worked example ($60,000 goal, 25% reserve, $6,000 expenses, 10% margin, 25 billable hours × 48 weeks = 1,200 hours): required revenue $95,555.56, floor rate $79.63 an hour, full-capacity monthly retainer $7,962.96, day rate $637.04 — all four match the live calculator page exactly. Tax figures: self-employment tax 15.3% on 92.35% of net earnings (about 14.13% effective), per the IRS and the calculator's own documentation; the 25–30% reserve is a planning range, not a tax calculation. Retainer ranges are typical monthly figures reported across 2026 freelancer pricing guides, not verified market data. Cross-checks: the three-retainer capacity total of $96,000 a year sits $444.44 above the $95,555.56 required revenue; the $1,600 retainer is 20.09% of that revenue; the $19,200 annual value assumes twelve paid months. Competitor note: freelancermetrics.com (top result, updated Oct 14, 2026) prices a retainer from a floor rate plus a 15% priority premium with a $2,875 worked example and service-type ranges, but gives no multi-retainer capacity math, no rollover-debt pricing, and no tax reserve on the fee; hourtab.com covers three pricing methods and an 8-hour minimum engagement, but no capacity stacking and no renewal-raise math; blog.usafreelancecalculator.com gives a five-step method with a $1,800 example and a 5% discount calculation, but no overage month worked end-to-end and no quarterly effective-rate audit; tool.teamzlab.com prices support-level multipliers and a 5–15% discount, but never derives the floor rate from an income goal; whatshouldicharge.io, billed.app, and remogrid.com agree on 100–125% overage rates, no-rollover defaults, and $1,500–$5,000 typical ranges, but none tracks the effective rate across light and heavy months. This article is general information, not tax, legal, or financial advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. A freelance retainer is reserved capacity priced from your floor rate: 20 hours at $80 an hour is $1,600 a month, $1,840 with a 15% priority premium — and a 10% discount drops it to $72 an hour, below the floor you need to hit your income goal.
  2. Rollover and overage decide whether the fee survives the year: cap rollover at one month and 25% of the hours, or 5 banked hours will cost you $400 of value, and write an overage rate of your standard rate plus 10 to 20% into the agreement before the first invoice.
  3. A retainer is a slice of a fixed month: three retainers totalling 55 of 100 billable hours leave a $4,400-a-month baseline and $3,600 of project headroom, and the fee rises at renewal — 10% takes $1,600 to $1,760 a month, $1,920 more a year.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.

  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
